newsitem.title: USA: Waxman says tobacco papers suggest industry fraud.
newsitem.headline: Waxman says tobacco papers suggest industry fraud.

text.p: A leading anti-smoking lawmaker Thursday released what he called confidential industry documents that he said suggest cigarette makers may have schemed to "defraud and deceive" the public for decades.

Representative Henry Waxman, a California Democrat, made public a handful of the thousands of confidential documents from Liggett and Myers Tobacco Co. He said the documents from the 1960s and '70s showed disturbing patterns of "potentially criminal or fraudulent conduct" by the industry and its lawyers.

A spokesman for the parent company of Liggett, Brooke Group Ltd., declined to comment on the Waxman allegations. A spokesman for the Tobacco Institute, the Washington-based industry group, was not immediately available.

Breaking ranks with other tobacco companies, Liggett in March settled suits with several states and agreed to turn over confidential documents. They have not been made public pending decisions by judges on whether that would violate attorney-client privilege, as claimed by other cigarette makers.

Waxman said that claim of privilege was a sham, hiding the involvement of lawyers in what he alleged was "an elaborate scheme to defraud and deceive the American public for over 30 years" by blocking the company from talking about health risks or promoting a "safer" cigarette. He cited five court cases in which judges have reviewed confidential documents and said the documents fall outside the standard privilege.
Waxman made the accusations in a news conference and in a report released by the Democratic staff of the Committee on Government Reform and Oversight.

At least 36 state attorneys general have sued the tobacco industry, and settlement talks have hit a crucial stage. The first case, in Mississippi, is scheduled to go to trial early next month and Republican congressional leaders have warned that time is running out for lawmakers to act on any broad industry settlement, which would need approval from Congress.

One of the fiercest congressional critics of the industry, Waxman said he was making the documents public because if there was a settlement, he wants to ensure broad disclosure about the companies' past activities and require accountability for the sake of public health.

The office of Sen. Frank Lautenberg, a New Jersey Democrat, said he would announce that many of the states suing cigarette makers back a plan he is promoting to prevent the industry from getting unlimited liability protection from future product liability suits. Two other lawmakers also were to outline a proposal to limit youth access to tobacco.
Waxman said he was introducing a Tobacco Accountability Act, which would set up a five-member independent board to be appointed by the Secretary of Health and Human Services.

The board would not have regulatory authority but it would have subpoena powers to ensure that the industry made public all documents relating to the health effects of tobacco, the "manipulation or control" of nicotine, and the sale or marketing of tobacco products to children, he said.

He said the Liggett documents showed the lawyers invoked attorney-client privilege to shield the role they played. For instance, he quoted from one document in which Liggett's general counsel intervened to block marketing a safe cigarette because it could "result in infinite liability" by in effect admitting the regular product was unsafe.

He cited another document which he said showed attorneys censored Liggett's communication of health risks to doctors, or prevented the company from making public statement about health because of liability concerns.

Waxman said the Liggett documents were not the most crucial from the company. The papers he released did not include any of the 3,500 documents that describe Liggett's joint defence strategies with other tobacco companies.
